title: What inspired means
hook: all-scripture-is-God-breathed (2 Timothy 3:16) is read by some as word-for-word, by others as God working through human writers

segments.voice: Yesterday, how the Bible was gathered: letters read aloud in worship until the churches knew which books were theirs. Your line was the church read these. Did you read a sentence aloud? Day one thousand sixty-six.

Dust, shaped into a person, lying still on the ground. Not alive yet. Then, in the second chapter of Genesis, God leans close: "and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul." Dust, plus breath, equals someone. Hold on to that picture, because a short line in a letter that opens with Paul's name reaches for the same breath, and Christians read it in more than one way. Today's word: inspiration.

The word inspiration carries a picture of breath. The line is in the second letter to Timothy: "All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness." Behind the King James phrase is a Greek word, theopneustos, usually rendered God-breathed. So the picture is Genesis again. God breathes, and something lifeless comes alive. Notice what the verse spends its breath on. It doesn't explain how the breathing worked. It says what scripture is for: teaching, correcting, setting straight, training. The letter is written to Timothy, who, it says, has known the holy scriptures from a child. It's practical. And the how is where Christians read differently. Some Christians, often evangelical, stress that God guided the writers so closely that the very words are what God intended, and teach that the Bible is without error in all it affirms. Others put the weight on God working through human writers: their languages, their styles, their times, their personalities. Catholic teaching holds the two together: God is the author of scripture, the human writers are true authors too, and the books teach without error the truth God wanted written down for our salvation. Orthodox and Protestant teachers stand at different points along that line. Both sides lean on another verse, in the second letter of Peter: "holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost." Holy men, spoke. Moved by the Spirit. Divine and human in the same sentence. Christians argue about how much weight each half carries. They agree on the breath. A book that, they say, didn't just get written. It got breathed into.

Here's the practice: read the verse, on the breath. Settle, and breathe in. On the out-breath, say the first half quietly: all scripture is given by inspiration of God. Breathe in again. On the next out-breath: and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness. Then just breathe, and notice that every word you said rode out on air. If you pray, you can ask that the words you read be alive for you. If not, simply rest in the breath. The bell holds the time.
Inspiration. A breath word. In 2 Timothy, scripture is God-breathed, and useful for teaching and training.
Your line: god-breathed. Today, when you take a deep breath, let it remind you of that dust in Genesis, coming alive. Day one thousand sixty-six.

howItsDone: Christians call the Bible inspired, God-breathed; some, often evangelical, stress that its very words are without error, others stress God working through true human authors, and Catholic teaching affirms both.

notes: 'Inspiration means breathing in' is the plain sense of the English/Latin word (inspirare); flagged under the claims rule as an etymology. 'Theopneustos, usually rendered God-breathed' is attributed. Confirm.

Inerrancy described as held by 'some Christians, often evangelical', 'without error in all it affirms' (Chicago Statement wording, paraphrased). Catholic teaching (Dei Verbum 11: God as author, the human writers as true authors) paraphrased. Orthodox grouped with 'God working through human writers'; check the Orthodox placement is fair.
The letter is called 'one of Paul's letters' in the hook, following its opening (2 Timothy 1:1); authorship is debated by scholars. Consider 'a letter in Paul's name'.

Audit: 'clay' changed to 'dust' (Genesis 2:7 says dust of the ground); teach, howItsDone, myth and trapdoor no longer set Catholic teaching against inerrancy (Dei Verbum 11 affirms both true human authors and that the books teach without error the truth God willed for our salvation), and evangelical teaching is no longer framed as denying human authorship. Orthodox placement kept general.

Editor pass: hook names 2 Timothy as 'a letter that opens with Paul's name' (authorship debated) and drops the 'ever since' time claim; the etymology 'inspiration means breathing in' softened to 'carries a picture of breath' in teach, word and screen.
